source.title: Collective evolution of weights in wide neural networks

record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and tests a mean-field description of gradient descent on a one-dimensional free-knot spline model. It does not test the claim versions’ classification-error outcomes or their named benchmark, architecture, width, initialization, learning-rate, or normalization conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own spline-model training simulations and comparisons with its theoretical dynamics. These are recorded as findings about the claim’s broader subject, with versions ["none"], because they measure quadratic regression loss and stationary behavior rather than the behavior named in V1–V6. CIFAR, two-layer teacher-student width, residual shortcuts, initialization comparisons, learning-rate thresholds, and batch normalization are not tested.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes continuous-time gradient descent and tests a mean-field approximation using one-dimensional spline regression. Its stationary-point results do not test V2's teacher–student width comparison; its initialization-dependent trajectories do not test V4's activation-matched initialization or propagation across depth. No results measure the behaviors specified by V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors derive a large-width transport description of weight evolution and report good agreement with spline simulations for stationary points, stability, and convergence rates. The derivation is heuristic and does not establish universal convergence to global minima.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a mean-field transport equation and numerical gradient descent on a one-dimensional free-knot spline model; it does not use the benchmark classification recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: In the spline simulations, stability depends on which pointlike stationary distribution is approached; loss convergence slows as the frequency parameter k grows for the stated sine ground truths.

fits_no_version.finding: Atomic spline initializations approach stationary distributions. Small perturbations contract near the tested stable branch but spread near the unstable interior stationary point and approach a globally minimizing distribution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested spline regression model, convergence and escape from stationary distributions depend on their stability and the initial distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss convergence slows substantially as the frequency of the tested sinusoidal regression targets increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher-frequency targets can produce slower gradient-descent convergence in the tested spline regression setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Simulated regression loss agrees reasonably with the theoretical expansion about the specified global minimizer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The mean-field linearization predicts loss dynamics reasonably well in the tested spline regression example.

record.problems: The paper describes itself as written at a “physics level of rigor” and says it does not fill in all mathematical details. Numerical results are for a simplified one-dimensional spline model; the reported measures are regression loss and weight-distribution dynamics, not classification error on standard benchmarks. No uncertainty estimates are stated.

untested.parts: Training classification error in large convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including corrupted labels and model-size or training-recipe qualifications.
Spurious-minimum frequencies under standard initialization as teacher and student widths grow, and the effect of adding one or two student neurons.
Training degradation with depth, identity residual shortcuts, and the stated initialization exceptions.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation across layers, training speed and trainable depth, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
Discrete learning-rate stability thresholds, curvature changes, recovery, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup training without normalization.

record.verdict_notes: Stationary-point stability here concerns continuous-time weight-distribution dynamics, not a discrete learning-rate stability threshold. Regression loss alone is not grounds for exclusion; the decisive issue is that these experiments and arguments do not address the specific behaviors and comparisons in V1–V6.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification error, random or corrupted labels, network size, optimizer, and early stopping or regularization.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious minima frequency, and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth, batch normalization, residual shortcuts, ImageNet/CIFAR-10, and plain-network training.
Comparisons of initialization schemes, signal or gradient propagation across depth, and deep tanh or convolutional networks.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, sharpness, and divergence or recovery during training.
Batch normalization speed or learning-rate tolerance and Fixup residual-network training.

rows.subject: linear spline model (31)
rows.operation_detail: Numerical gradient descent from atomic initial weight distributions; trajectories converge to stationary atomic distributions.

conditions.value: p(c,h,0) = δ(c − c0)δ(h − h0), with various c0, h0

rows.measure: Convergence to stationary distributions, not classification error
rows.value: The simulations converge to stationary atomic distributions of one of the two described kinds.
rows.note: The reported outcome concerns stationary spline distributions; it does not measure classification error or benchmark performance.
rows.check: Add the ground truth f(x) = x². Atomic initializations converge to stationary atomic distributions, which does not establish any claim version.

rows.subject: linear spline model (31)
rows.operation_detail: Numerical gradient descent from small-variance distributions near pointlike stationary distributions.

conditions.value: small positive variance near a stationary point with h* = 1

rows.measure: Stability of the weight trajectories near the stationary point
rows.note: The measure is stability near a spline stationary point, not training classification error.
rows.check: Specify f(x) = x² and the tested stable stationary branch with negative c*. The text attributes contraction to c* < 0; h* = 1 alone is an incomplete description of the stability condition.

rows.subject: linear spline model (31)
rows.operation_detail: Numerical gradient descent from small-variance distributions near pointlike stationary distributions.
rows.measure: Stability and subsequent evolution of the weight trajectories
rows.value: The evolution is unstable: weights diverge rapidly along h and then form a curve approaching a globally minimizing distribution spread relatively uniformly over h ∈ [0, 1].
rows.note: The result concerns instability and convergence toward a minimizing spline distribution, not classification error.
rows.check: Correct c* from (4 + √5)/5 to (4 + √6)/5; h* = (√6 − 1)/5. Specify f(x) = x². Spreading along h is escape from an unstable stationary distribution, not learning-rate-induced divergence under V5.

rows.subject: linear spline model (31)
rows.operation_detail: Numerical gradient descent from p(c,h,0) = δ(c)1[0,1](h), compared with the small-c approximate dynamics.
rows.value: The simulations show a substantial convergence slowdown with growing k, in agreement with the theoretical prediction.
rows.note: The paper reports a slowdown across the stated regression targets but does not report classification error.
rows.check: The reported slowdown with target frequency is accurately summarized, but it does not measure initialization quality, trainable depth, or another specified version.

rows.subject: linear spline model without the linear weight c
rows.operation_detail: Numerical gradient descent near a global optimum; experimental loss compared with the theoretical expansion.
rows.value: The experimental loss shows reasonable agreement with the theoretical expansion.
rows.note: This is a regression-loss comparison near a global minimizer, not a classification-error result.
rows.check: Correct the initial density to 2 × 1_[0.3,0.8], meaning weights sampled uniformly on that interval, rather than 1/2 × 1_[0.3,0.8]. Remove the unsupported numbers_found value '1/1'. Agreement between simulated loss and a theoretical expansion does not test any version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
